record_type_quote: The present research examined early comprehension of words that were instantiated as competing video stimuli. We presented 6–16-month-old infants with a broad set of common words, such as “dog” and “car” (see Table 1 ). The words we tested had some overlap with previous work, but only one pair of nouns (hand-feet) had been tested before with young infants, as either still images or video clips ( Tincoff & Jusczyk, 2012 ). We also included two pairs of verbs, one of which was tested in Bergelson & Swingley (2013b) . Thus, this study set out to replicate the basic finding of previous work, i.e. that young infants understand common nouns, while also extending the range of the words tested, and their format of presentation. The present study also extends previous findings in its methods, utilizing a varied series of video stimuli over twelve trials.

targets.title: At 6-9 months, human infants know the meanings of many common nouns.

targets.title: The acquisition of abstract words by young infants.

targets.outcome_quote: While the study was not designed to test the difference between noun and verb acquisition, 6–9-month-olds did perform well on one of the two verb pairs ( hug - eat ), contrary to their poor performance on a broader set of non-nouns in a prior study ( Bergelson & Swingley, 2013 ). Whether infants’ apparent success on hug-eat represents random item variation, or a first fragile glimmer of infants’ understanding of these verbs, is unclear, particularly given infants’ failure to demonstrate understanding of kiss-drink here.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The authors explicitly contrast success on one verb pair with prior non-noun failure while another pair fails; they also confirm the age boost from this original. The broad sentence about confirming several patterns does not give an overall verdict on the entire replication of this paper. Agreement passage: Not unexpectedly, this ability increases with age, but perhaps less expectedly the rate with which it increases is non-linear. This is the third study that finds evidence of a boost in performance around 13-14 months, independent of word type ( Bergelson & Swingley, 2012 , 2013b ).

New infant sample retests early lexical comprehension with moving images and additional items; five originals are explicitly linked to confirmed patterns and described individually in the introduction. The 2013b paper is separately retested on the age boost and overlapping verb stimuli; its contrasted non-noun result is retained rather than treating every citation as unqualified success. Other references supply background or measures. Publication is online 2014 and issue 2015; this is not an identity mismatch.
